Verify with a paper exercise: given a fictional exposure assessment scenario and monitoring data (including air and drinking water indicators), write the investigation hypotheses, exposure pathways, data verification steps, possible risk judgments and evidence gaps, and which conclusions must be made only after review by qualified professionals.

Signals worth considering: willingness to work with and verify exposure and monitoring data, to write scientific conclusions into reviewable reports, to accept alternating laboratory, field, and desk work, and to state things faithfully when evidence is insufficient. Signals requiring caution: unwillingness to record according to methods, inability to accept field and protection requirements, or expecting the work to be mainly clinical practice.
This card is a career exploration reference and does not constitute a hiring, competency scoring, or environmental and health conclusion.

First judge whether you can turn exposure and monitoring data into reviewable conclusions, write hypotheses and evidence clearly, and accept review, then judge whether you accept a way of working that alternates laboratory, field, and desk work and requires engaging with standards and permits; use the paper exercise and seven-day task on this page to verify, rather than looking only at the words "environmental" or "health."

The daily work of environmental scientists and specialists (including health) revolves around exposure and risk: conducting research and investigations, identifying pollutants and hazards affecting the environment and population health, collecting and analyzing air, water, soil, food, and workplace data, assessing exposure pathways and possible effects, reviewing permits and related materials, and writing the conclusions into reviewable reports.

U.S. O*NET-SOC 19-2041.00 "Environmental Scientists and Specialists, Including 
Health": conduct research and investigations to identify, reduce, or eliminate pollutants and hazards affecting the environment or public health; apply multidisciplinary knowledge to collect, synthesize, study, and report measurement or observation data and recommend actions. "Including Health" in the title means the scope covers research on hazards affecting population health and does not include clinical practice.
